articles.title: Rigorous analysis confirms NASA's Artemis II heat shield performance
articles.description: NASA's Artemis II mission sent four astronauts around the moon and brought them safely back to Earth, laying a foundation for crewed flights to the moon's surface.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Rigorous analysis confirms that NASA's Artemis II heat shield performed flawlessly, successfully protecting astronauts on their lunar journey. This validation represents a landmark achievement for humanity's return to the Moon.

articles.title: James Webb reveals a massive cosmic structure that challenges our understanding of the Universe
articles.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging existing models of cosmic structure formation. This discovery provides crucial new data for understanding how the universe assembled its largest structures.

articles.title: IceCube, high-energy neutrinos, and Francis Halzen win 2026’s Physics Nobel
articles.description:
Back in 1988, Francis Halzen had what he called a “cute idea.” His vision grew into the IceCube observatory, and earns the 2026 Nobel…
Continue reading on Starts With A Bang! »
articles.summary: Francis Halzen's groundbreaking IceCube neutrino observatory wins the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, validating decades of pioneering work in high-energy cosmic particle detection. This achievement opens revolutionary new windows for observing the universe.

articles.title: NASA to Help Unlock Mysteries of Mars’ Moons in Upcoming Mission
articles.description: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA’s (Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency) MMX (Martian Moons eXploration) mission, to advance our understanding of Mars’ moons and build on the agency’s long history of exploring the Red Planet. The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Mars’ moons Phobos and Deimos and deliver a sample […]
articles.summary: NASA partners with Japan's JAXA on the MMX mission to explore and unlock the mysteries of Mars' moons, advancing our understanding of the Red Planet's celestial companions.

articles.title: Mars moon lander set to launch on 19 October
articles.description:
The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is set to launch into space on a H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center at 04:41 JST on 20 October 2026 (20:41 BST / 21:41 CEST on 19 October 2026). MMX will be the first mission to collect a sample from Mars’s moon Phobos and bring it back to Earth. 
MMX is led by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), in collaboration with the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), the French space agency (CNES), the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and the European Space Agency (ESA).
articles.summary: The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is set to launch on October 19 aboard Japan's H3 rocket, beginning an exciting journey to study Mars's mysterious moons.

articles.title: Solar Orbiter tracks origin of mysterious magnetic switchbacks
articles.description: The European Space Agency-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft has flown through an S-shaped kink known as a ‘switchback’ in the solar wind’s magnetic field. By fingerprinting the elusive particles within the switchback, Solar Orbiter has traced its origin back to the Sun’s surface and revealed more about solar magnetism – the unruly instigator of dangerous solar storms.
articles.summary: The ESA's Solar Orbiter has flown through a mysterious magnetic switchback feature in the solar wind, revealing new insights into the Sun's dynamic magnetic behavior.

articles.title: Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.description:
Image:
			Webb captures commotion from nebula’s stellar jets
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope captures stunning imagery of a nebula's powerful stellar jets, revealing the dynamic processes of star formation.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The European-Chinese Smile mission begins its scientific operations to study how Earth's magnetosphere responds to solar wind interactions.

articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals distant galaxies in remarkable detail through gravitational lensing, acting as a cosmic magnifying glass to explore the early universe.

articles.title: Scientists Detect Rare Type of Wood Alcohol in Space
articles.description: As part of the ALMA COMPASS Large program, an international research team has detected a rare form of methanol in space for the first time.
articles.summary: An international research team using ALMA has detected a rare form of methanol in space, expanding our understanding of complex molecules in the cosmos. This discovery advances our knowledge of chemistry in interstellar environments.

articles.title: Host Stars Shape Their Planetary Systems Into Two Families
articles.description: New research draws a link between a host star and the characteristics of its planetary system. Higher mass stars create one family of systems, while lower mass stars create another. These results provide a new, more detailed template for understanding exoplanet systems.
articles.summary: New research demonstrates that a host star's mass directly influences the characteristics and organization of its planetary systems. This finding provides crucial insights into planetary system formation and diversity.

articles.title: SPHEREx Just Took the Fingerprints of Failed Stars Across Our Cosmic Neighborhood
articles.description: Brown dwarfs are the black (or brown?) sheep of astronomy. They’re too big to be considered a traditional gas planet, but they are too small to have started nuclear fusion and made the full transition to star-hood. They also change dramatically over time, cooling, shrinking, and spinning faster as they age. Or at least we think they do - our models of the atmospheres of these celestial objects aren’t the best, according to a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by a team led by Zafar Rustamkulov at Caltech and NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
articles.summary: The SPHEREx mission has successfully captured infrared signatures of brown dwarfs in our cosmic neighborhood. This achievement advances our understanding of substellar objects and their properties.

articles.title: The Perseverance Rover Reaches Another Milestone
articles.description: NASA's Perseverance Rover has reached another milestone. It now holds the record for the longest distance travelled on another world, meaning Mars and Earth's Moon. It's all thanks the ingenuity behind AutoNav, it's hazard-detection driving system. It's a win for science, as more distance travelled means more scientific objectives are reached.
articles.summary: NASA's Perseverance Rover has set a new record for the longest distance traveled on another planet. This milestone demonstrates humanity's remarkable achievements in Mars exploration.

articles.title: Astronomers Uncover More Intriguing Detail in an Ancient Supernova Remnant
articles.description: When a supernova exploded in 1181, Chinese and Japanese sky-watchers recorded it. They couldn't have known what the object was, and why it appeared for six months then disappeared. But in our modern times, we know it was a supernova, and we've even, most likely, found its remnant. New observations reveal more detail than ever in the unusual and rare supernova remnant.
articles.summary: Astronomers have uncovered new details in an ancient supernova remnant first observed in 1181 by Asian sky-watchers. Modern observations reveal the dynamic processes and evolution of this cosmic structure.

articles.title: Chandrasekhar Placed A Limit On White Dwarfs, But A New Study Finds This Limit Is Not Absolute
articles.description: The Chandrasekhar limit states that a white dwarf can be no larger than 1.4 solar masses. A new study demonstrates how highly magnetized white dwarfs could overcome that limit, and how such super-Chandrasekhar white dwarfs could form.
articles.summary: A groundbreaking study challenges the classical Chandrasekhar limit for white dwarfs, revealing that these stellar remnants can exceed previously thought constraints. This discovery expands our understanding of stellar physics.

articles.title: How did Mars get its moons? Japan's MMX space mission aims to solve the puzzle
articles.description: The Earth got its moon when a small planet collided with our planet more than 4 billion years ago. This impact hurled molten rock into space, which eventually coalesced to form the satellite we can see every night from across our planet.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Japan's MMX space mission aims to uncover the origin of Mars's moons through direct exploration. This ambitious mission will answer long-standing questions about planetary moon formation.

articles.title: Chandra breaks down 'Treble Clef's' galaxy cluster collision
articles.description: Astronomers have used NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory to break down the cause of a remarkable formation of radio waves they have nicknamed the "Treble Clef" because its distinct shape strongly resembles the musical symbol.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory reveals the mechanisms behind the remarkable 'Treble Clef' galaxy cluster collision and its associated radio wave formation. This analysis illuminates the dramatic interactions between massive cosmic structures.

articles.title: New evidence points to two feeding black holes just 175 parsecs apart lurking in the early universe
articles.description: Astronomers have found two actively feeding supermassive black holes separated by just 175 parsecs (570 light-years) in a galaxy seen when the universe was only about 2 billion years old. The system, MG B2016+112, lies at a redshift of 3.273 and is the most compact dual AGN known at this redshift. The study was posted to the arXiv preprint server on Sept. 25.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered two actively feeding supermassive black holes separated by only 175 parsecs in the early universe, offering rare insights into binary black hole systems. This finding challenges our understanding of how black holes interact and evolve in the cosmos.

articles.title: Scientists make stunning discovery that could help explain why life exists
articles.description: Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants may be finely balanced to make life possible. Even tiny changes to these constants could make liquids too thick or too thin for essential biological processes, potentially preventing life as we know it. Surprisingly, these life-friendly conditions existed billions of years before living cells appeared. The findings raise intriguing questions about why the laws of physics seem so well suited to life.
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that the universe's fundamental physical constants appear finely balanced to enable life, suggesting our cosmos may be uniquely suited for biological complexity. This finding deepens our understanding of why life can exist in our universe.

articles.title: Astronomers discover the 1st ever green star, a cosmic zombie just in time for Halloween
articles.description: Imagine if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween. Scientists have discovered that our star may go green if it turns into a cosmic zombie after its death in billions of years.
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered the first-ever green star, a rare binary system where a white dwarf's atmosphere absorbs red light to produce a striking green appearance. This unprecedented find expands our knowledge of stellar diversity and extreme cosmic objects.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
articles.description: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
articles.summary: On October 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini-Huygens probe on its groundbreaking 7-year voyage to Saturn. This historic mission would go on to revolutionize our understanding of Saturn, its rings, and its moons.

articles.title: Scientists discover 'chemical starter kit' for life in planetary birthplaces
articles.description: The discovery of surprising molecules of methanol and associated maser activity has expanded the inventory of the chemical starter kit that builds planets in young star systems.
articles.summary: Scientists have identified methanol and maser activity in star-forming regions, expanding our understanding of the chemical building blocks necessary for life. This discovery illuminates how habitable worlds may emerge throughout the universe.

articles.title: A-B Tech student experiment heads to International Space Station on board SpaceX rocket
articles.description: An A-B Tech student-led experiment was taken to the International Space Station aboard the SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket seen shooting through the sky early Tuesday morning.
articles.summary: A student-led experiment reaches the International Space Station aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, inspiring the next generation of space scientists. This mission demonstrates how educational initiatives drive innovation in human spaceflight.

articles.summary: Astronomy Picture of the Day features imagery of chasing the International Space Station, showcasing humanity's orbital outpost and space exploration achievements.

articles.title: Power Up: Roll Out Solar Arrays Boost Space Station Power Supply
articles.description: From the International Space Station’s unique position 250 miles above Earth, the Sun is a vital source of energy. Solar power supports the station’s life support systems, daily activities, and hundreds of research investigations that improve life on Earth and prepare humans for deep space exploration. Over the past five years, NASA augmented the station’s […]
articles.summary: The International Space Station deploys enhanced solar arrays to boost its power supply, improving the orbiting laboratory's capabilities for scientific research and exploration.

articles.title: NASA Welcomes All Ages, Experience Levels for Space Apps Challenge
articles.description: Registration is open for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, a two-day global event on Saturday, Nov. 14 and Sunday, Nov. 15, where teams work to create solutions inspired by NASA’s most ambitious exploration goals and making use of the agency’s free and open data. The annual challenge, often called a hackathon, is an intensive, […]
articles.summary: NASA opens registration for the 2026 Space Apps Challenge, a global two-day event welcoming participants of all ages and experience levels to innovate and solve space-related challenges.

articles.title: NASA Awards Enable Research, Technology to Build Future Workforce
articles.description: NASA has selected 12 U.S. institutions to receive $12 million to accelerate academic research and technology development in support of the agency’s priorities for exploring the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Through NASA’s Minority University Research and Education Project (MUREP) Space Technology Artemis Research (M‑STAR) initiative, selected institutions will each receive up to $1 million […]
articles.summary: NASA awards $12 million to 12 U.S. institutions to accelerate academic research and technology development, building the future workforce for space exploration.

articles.title: Mars’s oddest cloud may be even odder than we thought
articles.description: Scientists using the European Space Agency's Mars Express, in combination with a state-of-the-art meteorological model of the Red Planet, have found that there may be some very exotic physics behind Mars’s most curious cloud.
articles.summary: Scientists using ESA's Mars Express and advanced meteorological models discover that Mars's mysterious cloud formation is even more intriguing than previously thought.

articles.title: A galaxy spinning out of sync
articles.description:
Image:
			
Though the spiral galaxy in this new image by the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope seems serene, it hides a chaotic secret. This galaxy is NGC 4698, and it lies about 55 million light-years away in the constellation Virgo. It’s one of over one thousand galaxies in the Virgo Cluster, the nearest large cluster of galaxies bound together by gravity.
As a spiral galaxy similar to our own Milky Way galaxy, NGC 4698 has spiral arms that curl around within a thin disc of stars, gas and dust. Its centre is dominated by a galactic bulge.
The diffuse off-white glow of the galaxy’s bulge comes from stars smaller, older, and cooler than the massive blue stars that dot the galaxy’s outer disc. These tightly packed stars orbit a supermassive black hole containing millions of times the Sun’s mass. Scientists have found signs that this black hole is actively growing, drawing gas inward with its gravitational pull.
With a flat, starry disc and diffusely glowing centre, NGC 4698 looks a lot like a typical spiral galaxy — but this galaxy is far from normal. NGC 4698 is one of only a few known spiral galaxies with a bulge that extends out from the disc at a right angle. The elongation is faintly visible in this Hubble image, which shows the ghostly glow of the starry bulge peeking above and below the dusty disc. What’s more, the stars and gas nearest the galaxy’s centre rotate perpendicular to the rest of the disc.
What could cause a galaxy to be so out of sync? Astronomers have found that the culprit likely lies outside the galaxy. If NGC 4698 funneled in gas from an outside source, the newly collected gas could have formed a disc of gas and stars in the galaxy’s centre, at an angle relative to the rest of the disc. Some observations suggest that this galaxy once experienced a minor galactic merger, as evidenced by a short ‘tail’ of hydrogen streaming from one side of the galaxy.
The data used to create this image come from an observing programme (#18103; PI: Thilker) focusing on galaxies in the Virgo Cluster.
[Image Description: A spiral galaxy viewed at an angle, with a bright central bulge and winding spiral arms. The arms form a ring around the galaxy, without appearing to reach its centre. Prominent red-brown dust lanes weave through the arms, which are also dotted with bright blue and reddish regions of star formation. The galaxy is set against a dark background scattered with stars and faint distant galaxies.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The Hubble Space Telescope captures a fascinating spiral galaxy with unexpected rotational characteristics. This discovery reveals complex dynamics in galactic structure and evolution.

articles.title: Astronomers Observe The Limb Darkening Effect On Nearby Stars
articles.description: The edge of the Sun appears darker than its central region. This effect is known as limb darkening and tells us about the solar atmosphere. This same limb darkening effect has now been observed on several nearby stars and could help us improve our understanding of stellar atmospheres.
articles.summary: Astronomers have observed the limb darkening effect on nearby stars, providing insights into stellar atmospheres and composition. This research enhances our understanding of star physics.
